Mixed-effects models in table_regression()

Source: R/table_regression_mixed.R
table_regression_mixed.Rd

table_regression() reads the mixed-effects fits of lme4::lmer(), lme4::glmer(), glmmTMB::glmmTMB() and nlme::lme(), and the generalized least squares fits of nlme::gls(). The fixed effects fill the coefficient rows. The variance components follow them as a Random effects block of rows, in the same columns. The number of groups, the ICC and the marginal and conditional R-squared of Nakagawa are fit-statistic rows, and the note gives the likelihood-ratio test of the whole random part. Cumulative-link mixed models (ordinal::clmm(), and glmmTMB() with family = glmmTMB::ordinal()) get the same block of rows; their other rules are those of the ordinal models, in table_regression_ordinal.

Usage

table_regression(
  models,
  show_re = TRUE,
  re_scale = c("sd", "variance"),
  re_columns = c("est", "se", "ci"),
  re_test = c("none", "lrt", "rlrt"),
  re_ci = c("wald", "profile"),
  ...  # the arguments of every class: see ?table_regression
)

The other arguments are documented in table_regression(); the values they take for mixed models are listed below.

Engines

ClassEngineAMEExponentiateBlocksvcov
lmerModlme4::lmer()yes-Random effectsclassical, CR0-CR3
glmerModlme4::glmer()yesOR / IRR (link)Random effectsclassical
glmmTMBglmmTMB::glmmTMB()yes (no for the ordinal family)link-dependent (IRR for count families, OR for ordinal logit)Random effects; Zero-inflation; Zero hurdle, Pr(y = 0) for a zero-truncated family, ziGamma, lognormal or beta_family; Dispersion; Thresholds (ordinal family)classical, CR0, CR1 (classical only for REML or the ordinal family)
lmenlme::lme()yes-Random effectsclassical, CR0-CR3 (classical only with contrasts other than the session's)
glsnlme::gls()yes--classical

AME: whether the average-marginal-effects columns are available. Exponentiate: what exponentiate = TRUE gives. Blocks: the labeled blocks of rows the class adds below its coefficients. vcov: the values of vcov the class accepts. The same rows are returned by subset(table_regression_models(), family == "Mixed effects").

What the table shows

Coefficient rows. One row per fixed-effect coefficient, as for lm and glm. Under exponentiate = TRUE a glmer or glmmTMB fit follows the link rules of glm: odds ratios under the logit link, rate ratios under the log link, an error for a link whose exponential is not a ratio. The rows are conditional on a random effect of zero: an exponentiated intercept is the baseline odds or rate of a group whose random effect is zero, not the average over groups.

Random-effects rows. One row per standard deviation and per correlation of each grouping factor, then the residual of a Gaussian model, each with its estimate, SE and CI in the coefficient columns. The rows of a glmer or glmmTMB fit are on the scale of the linear predictor (log-odds, log-rate). The rows carry no p-value: a Wald test of a variance is invalid at the boundary of its parameter space (Self & Liang 1987), and re_test adds a test that is valid there. The note gives the estimation method (REML or ML) and the likelihood-ratio test of the whole random part against the model without random effects, with its boundary-corrected chi-bar-squared p-value (Self & Liang 1987; Stram & Lee 1994). For an lme fit the null model keeps the residual variance and correlation structure of the fit. A gls fit has no random effects and no block. glmmTMB zero-inflation, hurdle and dispersion components render as further blocks, described in table_regression_counts (show_components).

In broom::tidy() the variance-component rows have estimate_type = "vc", their terms are prefixed re::, and the correlations carry a ::cor suffix.

Fit statistics. By default, n, one N (<group>) row per grouping factor ("n_groups"), the ICC, the marginal and conditional R-squared, AIC and BIC; see Fit statistics below.

Arguments for this family

These arguments act on the random-effects rows only. They have no effect on fits without random effects.

show_re

Logical. TRUE (default) renders the Random effects block for lmer, glmer, glmmTMB, lme and clmm fits. FALSE suppresses it. re_test and re_ci = "profile" need the block and are refused with show_re = FALSE.

re_scale

"sd" (default) or "variance". "sd" reports the standard deviation \(\sigma\), in the units of the linear predictor (those of the outcome for a Gaussian model). "variance" reports \(\sigma^2\), in squared units. The standard error is a delta-method one on the scale the engine estimates on, and \(SE(\sigma) = SE(\sigma^2) / (2\sigma)\). For lmer and glmer it comes from the covariance matrix of the variances (merDeriv). For lme, glmmTMB and clmm the engine estimates \(\log\sigma\) and the SE is \(\sigma \, SE(\log\sigma)\). The Wald CI of every engine is built on \(\log\sigma\), \(\sigma \exp(\pm z \, SE(\log\sigma))\), and squared for \(\sigma^2\): by spicy for lmer and glmer, by the engine otherwise (nlme::intervals(), glmmTMB::confint()). The residual row of a Gaussian glmmTMB fit has its SE and CI too. Correlation rows (\(\rho\)) have no unit and are unchanged. Their SE is a delta-method one too: from the variances for lmer (CI \(\rho \pm z \, SE\), clamped to \([-1, 1]\)), from \(\mathrm{atanh}(\rho)\) for lme, and from glmmTMB's \(\rho / \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\) in a two-term block, with the engine's CI. In a glmmTMB block of three terms or more it is the width of glmmTMB's interval divided by \(2z\).

re_columns

Subset of c("est", "se", "ci"): the cells of the random-effects rows that are displayed ("est" is mandatory). Deselected cells render as an en dash on those rows only: re_columns = "est" for estimates alone, c("est", "se") for a journal that wants standard errors only. Display only: broom::tidy() and as_structured() keep the SE and CI.

re_test

"none" (default), "lrt" or "rlrt". A per-term test of the variance components, which fills the p column of the random-effects rows. Both are likelihood-ratio tests; a Wald test of a variance is refused (see What is refused, and why).

  • "lrt": likelihood-ratio test of each random term against the model refitted without it (its variance and its covariances with the other terms of its bar), referred to the chi-bar-squared mixture 0.5 chi2(q-1) + 0.5 chi2(q) (Self & Liang 1987; Stram & Lee 1994). The reduction scheme is that of lmerTest::ranova(), and the mixture makes the p-value asymptotically exact instead of conservative. The intercept of a bar is tested only when it is the only term of the bar. Available for lmer, glmer, glmmTMB, and lme with a simple random = ~ terms | group structure.

  • "rlrt": exact restricted likelihood-ratio test with a simulated finite-sample null (RLRsim::exactRLRT(); Crainiceanu & Ruppert 2004). Defined only for a Gaussian lmer or lme fit with a single variance component; other fits are refused with a pointer to "lrt".

The statistic and its df stay out of the t/z column (they are on the chi-square scale) and are kept in broom::tidy() (test_type "chibar2" or "rlrt"). The test of the whole block in the note is unchanged. Correlation and residual rows are never tested. Each random term costs one refit; a refit that fails leaves its row untested, with a spicy_fallback warning. For other structures, pbkrtest::PBmodcomp() gives a parametric-bootstrap test of the same pair of fits (Halekoh & Højsgaard 2014), to report beside the table.

re_ci

"wald" (default) or "profile": the uncertainty of the random-effects rows of lmer and glmer fits.

  • "wald": SE from the information matrix (merDeriv, expected information by default) and a Wald CI symmetric on the log of the standard deviation, which stays above 0 (see re_scale). Wald can be optimistic near the boundary of a variance; "profile" respects it. Its cost grows faster than the number of observations (about a minute at n of roughly 2,700). Above options("spicy.re_se_max_n") (default 1000) the SE and CI are skipped: the rows keep their estimates, the cells show an en dash, a note states the omission and a spicy_caveat warning is raised. Raise the cap (options(spicy.re_se_max_n = Inf)) to force the computation, or use re_ci = "profile".

  • "profile": profile-likelihood intervals from confint(fit, method = "profile"), the route lme4 documents. They are asymmetric and respect the boundary at 0. No SE is shown, since a symmetric SE misdescribes the skewed sampling distribution of a variance. There is no size cap (about two seconds per variance parameter at n of 7,000; more for glmer). The note names the method, and re_scale = "variance" shows the profile interval of the variance itself.

glmmTMB, lme and clmm fits keep the intervals of their own engine under "wald" (see re_scale) and refuse "profile".

The arguments shared with other classes take these values for mixed models:

vcov, cluster

lmer and lme: "classical" and "CR0" to "CR3". glmmTMB: "classical", "CR0" and "CR1". glmer and gls: "classical" only. See Standard errors, degrees of freedom and intervals.

ci_method

"wald" only. "profile" is defined for glm and the ordinal models, and "boot_percentile" needs vcov = "bootstrap", which mixed models refuse. The intervals of the random-effects rows are set by re_ci.

standardized

"refit": the model is refitted on z-scored data with its random structure, the one approach that is well posed for a mixed model, since the marginal SD(y) has no unique decomposition across levels. "posthoc", "basic", "smart" and "pseudo" fall back to "refit" with a spicy_fallback warning. The \(\beta\) rows take the reference distribution of their B rows, so B and \(\beta\) carry the same p-value, and a robust vcov is applied to the refit too. A formula with an inline transform (log(x), poly()) cannot be refitted: the \(\beta\) rows are left out, with a warning; build the transformed column in data before fitting. Refused for glmmTMB with the ordinal family, whose outcome has no scale.

show_columns

"partial_chi2" is the Wald chi-square of each term, Type II by default and Type III under partial_type = "III" (the type SAS PROC MIXED and lmerTest report; the two agree for a model without interactions). It follows the robust vcov when one is set. "partial_f" and the variance-explained partials ("partial_f2", "partial_eta2", "partial_omega2") are not defined. The AME tokens are available for every engine of the table above except glmmTMB with the ordinal family; no column token is reserved to mixed models.

show_fit_stats

Four tokens belong to this family: "n_groups" (also used by GEE and fixest fits), "icc", "r2_marginal" and "r2_conditional". See Fit statistics.

Standard errors, degrees of freedom and intervals

The fixed effects are tested as each engine tests them:

  • A fit of lmerTest::lmer(): t with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

  • A plain lme4::lmer() fit: Wald z. A message, once per session, suggests refitting with lmerTest::lmer(); the note names the method only.

  • glmer and glmmTMB: Wald z.

  • lme: t with the containment degrees of freedom of nlme, named in the note. gls: t on n minus the number of coefficients.

The confidence interval uses the same reference distribution as the test. The AME rows take the variance matrix of the coefficient rows, model-based or robust, and are tested by Wald z. Beside the t rows of an lmerTest or lme fit, or of a CR* variance, an identity-link AME can therefore carry another p-value than the B of the same row; read it as a large-sample approximation.

Cluster-robust variance. lmer and lme fits take "CR0" to "CR3" from clubSandwich::vcovCR(), with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom computed from the robust matrix. An lme fitted with other contrasts than those of the session is refused: clubSandwich rebuilds its design with the session contrasts, so its variance would not match the coefficients. glmmTMB fits take "CR0" and "CR1" from glmmTMB's own sandwich (glmmTMB >= 1.1.15), which covers the coefficients, the zero-inflation and dispersion blocks and the AME. "CR0" is the sandwich as glmmTMB computes it, with one score per cluster (the gradient of the marginal log-likelihood of the cluster); "CR1" scales it by \(G/(G-1)\), G the number of clusters. Both use Wald z. Without cluster, the cluster is the top-level grouping factor of the random effects. The estimator needs independent clusters that contain the random effects, every group within one cluster, so crossed random effects need a cluster that contains them all. It keeps the standard errors valid when the random-effects distribution or the conditional variance is misspecified, provided the estimates stay consistent (Liang & Zeger 1986 for a misspecified variance and correlation, Verbeke & Lesaffre 1997 for the random-effects distribution). With few clusters it understates the variance, which the factor of "CR1" offsets only in part: this class has no bias-reduced correction (Cameron & Miller 2015).

The robust estimator covers the fixed effects: their coefficients, their joint tests ("partial_chi2"), the standardized coefficients and the AME. The variance components keep their model-based inference. glmmTMB's sandwich takes one likelihood score per cluster over the fixed and variance parameters, while the CR* estimators of lmer and lme come from clubSandwich over the fixed effects alone: on the same model the two agree as the clusters grow, but not exactly.

Hierarchical comparison (nested = TRUE). The default change rows are c("aic_change", "bic_change", "lrt_change", "p_change") (Pinheiro & Bates 2000, Section 2.4.1), from the engine's own two-model anova(). Under "CR0" to "CR3", lmer and lme hierarchies use the HTZ test of clubSandwich::Wald_test(); under "CR0" and "CR1", a glmmTMB hierarchy uses a Wald chi-square. See Hierarchical (nested) model comparison in table_regression().

Fit statistics

By default, c("nobs", "n_groups", "icc", "r2_marginal", "r2_conditional", "aic", "bic"), for lmer, glmer, glmmTMB, lme and clmm fits. A row of the default that no model of the table fills is left out. A token named in the call that no model fills is refused. A gls fit gets n and AIC.

  • "n_groups": one N (<group>) row per grouping factor.

  • "icc": the intraclass correlation of a model with one random intercept and no other random term: \(\sigma^2_u / (\sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_e)\). For a non-Gaussian glmer fit the residual variance is the distribution variance of the link scale (the adjusted ICC of Nakagawa, Johnson & Schielzeth 2017): \(\pi^2/3\) for the logit, 1 for the probit, \(\pi^2/6\) for the cloglog, and \(\log(1 + 1/\lambda)\) for a Poisson log fit. A binomial cbind() response, whose rows are not single trials, has no ICC. For glmmTMB the ICC is computed for the Gaussian identity family only. A model with random slopes has no ICC: its cell is empty. With several grouping factors there is no single ICC, and the note says so.

  • "r2_marginal", "r2_conditional": the R-squared of Nakagawa & Schielzeth (2013), the variance explained by the fixed effects alone and by the fixed and random effects together; the values match performance::r2_nakagawa(). Empty for gls.

  • On request: "deviance", "log_lik" (the restricted log-likelihood of a REML fit), "sigma" (see Vocabulary tokens in table_regression() for its glmmTMB families), and the dispersion rows of a negative-binomial or beta family ("theta", "alpha", "delta", "phi").

  • Refused when every model of the table is mixed: "r2", "adj_r2", "omega2", "f2", the pseudo-R-squared tokens and "r2_deviance". They have no definition for a mixed model; the error points to "r2_marginal" and "r2_conditional".

What is refused, and why

  • HC*, "bootstrap" and "jackknife" for every mixed engine: these estimators assume independent observations or refit lm and glm, and the random effects exist to model the dependence.

  • CR* for glmer (clubSandwich has no working backend for it), and "CR2" and "CR3" for glmmTMB (its sandwich has one score per cluster, with no residuals and no hat values). A robust vcov for a glmmTMB fit by REML or with the ordinal family.

  • A Wald test of a variance component, on any engine: the null value 0 lies on the boundary of the parameter space.

  • re_ci = "profile" outside lme4, and re_test = "rlrt" outside a Gaussian fit with one variance component.

  • Under nested = TRUE:

    • A REML pair whose fixed effects differ (nlme::lme(method = "REML"), glmmTMB(REML = TRUE)). The restricted likelihood depends on the fixed-effects design, so the likelihood-ratio test is not valid (Pinheiro & Bates 2000, Section 2.4.2). Refit both by maximum likelihood. A REML pair that differs only in its random structure stays valid.

    • Fits from different engines. No engine's anova() accepts a fit of another; refit one with the other's engine.

    • The variance-explained change tokens ("r2_change", "adj_r2_change", "f_change", "f2_change"). The comparison is a chi-square.

    nested = FALSE sets the models side by side instead.

References

Cameron, A.C. & Miller, D.L. (2015). A practitioner's guide to cluster-robust inference. Journal of Human Resources, 50(2), 317-372.

Crainiceanu, C.M. & Ruppert, D. (2004). Likelihood ratio tests in linear mixed models with one variance component. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 66(1), 165-185.

Halekoh, U. & Højsgaard, S. (2014). A Kenward-Roger approximation and parametric bootstrap methods for tests in linear mixed models: The R package pbkrtest. Journal of Statistical Software, 59(9). doi:10.18637/jss.v059.i09

Liang, K.-Y. & Zeger, S.L. (1986). Longitudinal data analysis using generalized linear models. Biometrika, 73(1), 13-22.

Nakagawa, S. & Schielzeth, H. (2013). A general and simple method for obtaining R2 from generalized linear mixed-effects models. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 4(2), 133-142.

Nakagawa, S., Johnson, P.C.D. & Schielzeth, H. (2017). The coefficient of determination R2 and intra-class correlation coefficient from generalized linear mixed-effects models revisited and expanded. Journal of the Royal Society Interface, 14(134), 20170213. doi:10.1098/rsif.2017.0213

Pinheiro, J.C. & Bates, D.M. (2000). Mixed-effects models in S and S-PLUS. Springer.

Self, S.G. & Liang, K.-Y. (1987). Asymptotic properties of maximum likelihood estimators and likelihood ratio tests under nonstandard conditions. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 82(398), 605-610.

Stram, D.O. & Lee, J.W. (1994). Variance components testing in the longitudinal mixed effects model. Biometrics, 50(4), 1171-1177.

Verbeke, G. & Lesaffre, E. (1997). The effect of misspecifying the random-effects distribution in linear mixed models for longitudinal data. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, 23(4), 541-556.

See also

table_regression() for the arguments shared by all classes; table_regression_models() for the registry of supported classes and the other families; table_regression_ordinal for the thresholds of clmm and of the ordinal family of glmmTMB; table_regression_counts for the zero-inflation, hurdle and dispersion blocks of glmmTMB; the Mixed-effects regression tables article.

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)) {
  fit <- lme4::lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (Days | Subject),
                    data = lme4::sleepstudy)
  print(table_regression(fit))

  # Variances instead of standard deviations, estimates only.
  print(table_regression(fit, re_scale = "variance", re_columns = "est"))

  # Nested comparison, fitted by maximum likelihood.
  m1 <- lme4::lmer(Reaction ~ 1 + (1 | Subject),
                   data = lme4::sleepstudy, REML = FALSE)
  m2 <- lme4::lmer(Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject),
                   data = lme4::sleepstudy, REML = FALSE)
  print(table_regression(list(m1, m2), nested = TRUE))
}
